query:
Context. We will ultrasonically atomize 1.1 kg of 70 wt% Cu / 30 wt% Ni (binary cupronickel, near
UNS C71500; liquidus ~1240 C, solidus ~1170 C) in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER. The charge is induction-melted
in a BN-coated crucible to roughly 1260-1300 C (the induction module's practical limit is ~1300 C), then
poured in argon through a bottom nozzle (BN stopper rod) onto a horizontal plate on an ultrasonic
sonotrode (1:1.5 booster, 100% generator amplitude). The plate is the atomizing surface: a thin melt
film on it is continuously renewed for the length of the pour, likely 5-30 minutes. The plate is a
carbon-fiber composite (probably carbon-carbon) that was "dipped" in molybdenum. A previous review
flagged the Mo coat as high risk: a Cu-32Ni melt dissolves ~3.7 wt% Mo at 1300 C (Teodorovich 1980,
doi:10.1007/bf00791375), and a Ni-rich alloy atomized on a solid Mo sonotrode in a rePOWDER picked up
~2.6 wt% Mo (Goncharov 2026, doi:10.3390/met16030318). A colleague now proposes a carbon-fiber plate
dipped in TUNGSTEN instead.

A separate, broader query is already comparing W and Mo qualitatively. For this one we need numbers
with sources, and physical estimates with the inputs shown where the literature is silent.

1. Solubility of W in the melt. Report the equilibrium solubility of W (wt% and at%) in liquid
   Cu-30Ni, and along the Cu-Ni join, at 1250, 1300 and 1350 C, from experimental Cu-Ni-W phase
   equilibria and CALPHAD assessments (name them and give their values). Cross-check against:
   (i) the Ni-W binary (W in liquid Ni near the ~1495 C peritectic; (Ni) dissolves ~17.5 at% W);
   (ii) Cu-W (W solubility in liquid Cu); (iii) the W content of the Ni-Cu matrix in
   liquid-phase-sintered W-Ni-Cu heavy alloys versus Ni:Cu ratio and sintering temperature;
   (iv) Mo in the same melts. At W saturation and 1250-1300 C, is the phase in equilibrium with the
   melt pure (W), a (Ni,W) fcc solid solution, or a Ni-W intermetallic (Ni4W, NiW)? Could a solid
   Ni-W-rich layer form and grow on the plate, raising the local liquidus and seeding freezing of
   the thin film?

2. Rate of attack. Give measured dissolution rate constants or recession rates of W, and of Mo for
   comparison, in liquid Ni, Cu-Ni or Ni-base melts (rotating-disc, immersion or diffusion-couple
   studies, e.g., W wire or W crucibles in Ni-base superalloy melts), and say whether dissolution is
   diffusion- or interface-controlled. Report what is known about ultrasonic or cavitation
   enhancement of dissolution and erosion of W, Mo, Nb, Ti or steel sonotrodes in metal melts. Then
   estimate, with stated assumptions, the recession depth (micrometres) at the melt impingement zone
   for a W coat and for a Mo coat during a 10-30 minute pour, and the resulting W or Mo content of
   the 1.1 kg of powder.

3. W coatings on carbon-fiber composites. Summarize precedents with numbers: the JET ITER-like wall W
   coatings on CFC (combined magnetron sputtering and ion implantation, ~10-25 um W on a Mo
   interlayer), vacuum-plasma-sprayed W on CFC or graphite, and CVD W on C/C. Give their adhesion,
   the thickness above which they delaminate, cracking under thermal cycling and high heat flux, the
   onset temperature and growth rate of W2C/WC at the W/C interface and its effect on adhesion,
   diffusion barriers (Re, Mo), and recrystallization and embrittlement of W coatings at 1200-1400 C.
   How would such coatings respond to sustained 20-60 kHz vibration at an atomizing plate's
   displacement amplitude?

4. What "dipping" in W can practically mean, since W melts at 3422 C: slurry or paint dip coats with
   sintering (temperatures; sintering aids such as Ni, Fe or Co that would themselves dissolve in
   Cu-Ni), molten-salt electrodeposition of W, CVD from WF6, chemical vapour infiltration, and thermal
   spray. Give typical thickness, density or porosity and adhesion for each, and say whether a porous
   W layer would be infiltrated by a Cu-Ni melt (W-Cu composites are made by infiltrating porous W
   with Cu, and Ni activates the wetting), giving the melt a path to the carbon.

5. Wetting. Contact angles of liquid Cu, Ni and Cu-Ni on W, on Mo and on graphite or carbon fiber at
   1100-1400 C in argon or vacuum, including the effect of surface oxides (WO2/WO3, MoO2/MoO3) and of
   Ni as a wetting activator. Is complete wetting desirable on an ultrasonic atomizing plate, or does
   it promote film pinning, infiltration and erosion?

6. Acoustics. For a thin plate on an ultrasonic horn, estimate the added mass and the
   resonant-frequency shift from a W coat versus a Mo coat of the same thickness (densities 19.3 and
   10.2 g/cm3; C/C ~1.6-1.9 g/cm3), for 25, 100 and 250 um per side on a 2-3 mm plate, and say
   whether a typical generator's frequency-tracking range would still lock. Comment on damping and
   heating in a porous coat.

7. Powder consequences. At the W pickup estimated in item 2, would W stay in solution in Cu-30Ni
   powder or appear as W particles, and what would it do to compliance with UNS C71500 (and the
   military specifications that cite it), to seawater corrosion, and to laser powder-bed fusion?

Finish with (a) a direct verdict on W versus Mo for this run, (b) a table of failure mode -> Mo coat
-> W coat (numbers where possible) -> mitigation, and (c) the plate you would choose for this run and
why (solid Mo or TZM, solid W or W-La2O3, W-coated Mo, or a ceramic such as BN, alumina, zirconia or
SiC-coated C/C), naming any ultrasonic-atomization or ultrasonic-melt-processing precedent for it.
task_summary: Quantitative Assessment Of Tungsten Versus Molybdenum Coatings For Ultrasonic Atomization Of Cu‑30Ni

info.name: clinical_trials_search

Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research
        - BASIC_SCIENCE: Basic Science
        - DEVICE_FEASIBILITY: Device Feasibility
        - OTHER: Other

    InterventionType:
        - BEHAVIORAL: Behavioral interventions
        - BIOLOGICAL: Biological interventions
        - COMBINATION_PRODUCT: Combination product interventions
        - DEVICE: Device interventions
        - DIAGNOSTIC_TEST: Diagnostic test interventions
        - DIETARY_SUPPLEMENT: Dietary supplement interventions
        - DRUG: Drug interventions
        - GENETIC: Genetic interventions
        - PROCEDURE: Procedure interventions
        - RADIATION: Radiation interventions
        - OTHER: Other interventions

    DesignAllocation:
        - RANDOMIZED: Randomized allocation

        - NA: Not applicable

    InterventionalAssignment:
        - SINGLE_GROUP: Single group assignment

    ObservationalModel:

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: paper_search
info.description:
Search for papers in Google Scholar for you to look at.

Can be called repeatedly with identical parameters to retrieve more results (max 2 repeats).
A short summary of the retrieved papers will be returned, but to examine the full content of each paper,
you must use the gather_evidence tool.

query.description:
A Google Scholar search query, which can be a specific phrase, complete sentence,
or general keywords, e.g. 'machine learning for immunology'. Also can be
given search operators like 'author:'.
query.title: Query

min_year.description:
filter for minimum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
min_year.title: Min Year

max_year.description:
filter for maximum publication year.
The current year is 2026. If unsure about time range, do not set.
max_year.title: Max Year

info.name: open_targets_search
info.description:
Search for disease-target associations from OpenTargets database.

Adds new disease-target association data to the state and returns top search results.

disease_names.description:
List of disease names to search for.
Usage:
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Returns top targets for Alzheimer's
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's", "Diabetes"], target_names = ["PSEN1"] ->
    Filters for only PSEN1-Alzheimer's/Diabetes evidence
disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
disease_names.title: Disease Names

target_names.description:
List of target names to search for.
Usage:
target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Returns top diseases associated with BACE1
target_names = ["BACE1", "APP"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for only these target-Alzheimer's pairs
target_names = ["BACE1"], drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
target_names.title: Target Names

drug_names.description:
List of drug names to generate or filter results.
Usage:
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"] ->
    Returns all disease-target pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], disease_names = ["Alzheimer's"] ->
    Filters for Alzheimer's pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names = ["Aducanumab"], target_names = ["BACE1"] ->
    Filters for BACE1 disease pairs treated by Aducanumab
drug_names.title: Drug Names

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,

Use the tools to answer the question: Context. We will ultrasonically atomize 1.1 kg of 70 wt% Cu / 30 wt% Ni (binary cupronickel, near
UNS C71500; liquidus ~1240 C, solidus ~1170 C) in an AMAZEMET rePOWDER. The charge is induction-melted
in a BN-coated crucible to roughly 1260-1300 C (the induction module's practical limit is ~1300 C), then
poured in argon through a bottom nozzle (BN stopper rod) onto a horizontal plate on an ultrasonic
sonotrode (1:1.5 booster, 100% generator amplitude). The plate is the atomizing surface: a thin melt
film on it is continuously renewed for the length of the pour, likely 5-30 minutes. The plate is a
carbon-fiber composite (probably carbon-carbon) that was "dipped" in molybdenum. A previous review
flagged the Mo coat as high risk: a Cu-32Ni melt dissolves ~3.7 wt% Mo at 1300 C (Teodorovich 1980,
doi:10.1007/bf00791375), and a Ni-rich alloy atomized on a solid Mo sonotrode in a rePOWDER picked up
~2.6 wt% Mo (Goncharov 2026, doi:10.3390/met16030318). A colleague now proposes a carbon-fiber plate
dipped in TUNGSTEN instead.

A separate, broader query is already comparing W and Mo qualitatively. For this one we need numbers
with sources, and physical estimates with the inputs shown where the literature is silent.

1. Solubility of W in the melt. Report the equilibrium solubility of W (wt% and at%) in liquid
   Cu-30Ni, and along the Cu-Ni join, at 1250, 1300 and 1350 C, from experimental Cu-Ni-W phase
   equilibria and CALPHAD assessments (name them and give their values). Cross-check against:
   (i) the Ni-W binary (W in liquid Ni near the ~1495 C peritectic; (Ni) dissolves ~17.5 at% W);
   (ii) Cu-W (W solubility in liquid Cu); (iii) the W content of the Ni-Cu matrix in
   liquid-phase-sintered W-Ni-Cu heavy alloys versus Ni:Cu ratio and sintering temperature;
   (iv) Mo in the same melts. At W saturation and 1250-1300 C, is the phase in equilibrium with the
   melt pure (W), a (Ni,W) fcc solid solution, or a Ni-W intermetallic (Ni4W, NiW)? Could a solid
   Ni-W-rich layer form and grow on the plate, raising the local liquidus and seeding freezing of
   the thin film?

2. Rate of attack. Give measured dissolution rate constants or recession rates of W, and of Mo for
   comparison, in liquid Ni, Cu-Ni or Ni-base melts (rotating-disc, immersion or diffusion-couple
   studies, e.g., W wire or W crucibles in Ni-base superalloy melts), and say whether dissolution is
   diffusion- or interface-controlled. Report what is known about ultrasonic or cavitation
   enhancement of dissolution and erosion of W, Mo, Nb, Ti or steel sonotrodes in metal melts. Then
   estimate, with stated assumptions, the recession depth (micrometres) at the melt impingement zone
   for a W coat and for a Mo coat during a 10-30 minute pour, and the resulting W or Mo content of
   the 1.1 kg of powder.

3. W coatings on carbon-fiber composites. Summarize precedents with numbers: the JET ITER-like wall W
   coatings on CFC (combined magnetron sputtering and ion implantation, ~10-25 um W on a Mo
   interlayer), vacuum-plasma-sprayed W on CFC or graphite, and CVD W on C/C. Give their adhesion,
   the thickness above which they delaminate, cracking under thermal cycling and high heat flux, the
   onset temperature and growth rate of W2C/WC at the W/C interface and its effect on adhesion,
   diffusion barriers (Re, Mo), and recrystallization and embrittlement of W coatings at 1200-1400 C.
   How would such coatings respond to sustained 20-60 kHz vibration at an atomizing plate's
   displacement amplitude?

4. What "dipping" in W can practically mean, since W melts at 3422 C: slurry or paint dip coats with
   sintering (temperatures; sintering aids such as Ni, Fe or Co that would themselves dissolve in
   Cu-Ni), molten-salt electrodeposition of W, CVD from WF6, chemical vapour infiltration, and thermal
   spray. Give typical thickness, density or porosity and adhesion for each, and say whether a porous
   W layer would be infiltrated by a Cu-Ni melt (W-Cu composites are made by infiltrating porous W
   with Cu, and Ni activates the wetting), giving the melt a path to the carbon.

5. Wetting. Contact angles of liquid Cu, Ni and Cu-Ni on W, on Mo and on graphite or carbon fiber at
   1100-1400 C in argon or vacuum, including the effect of surface oxides (WO2/WO3, MoO2/MoO3) and of
   Ni as a wetting activator. Is complete wetting desirable on an ultrasonic atomizing plate, or does
   it promote film pinning, infiltration and erosion?

6. Acoustics. For a thin plate on an ultrasonic horn, estimate the added mass and the
   resonant-frequency shift from a W coat versus a Mo coat of the same thickness (densities 19.3 and
   10.2 g/cm3; C/C ~1.6-1.9 g/cm3), for 25, 100 and 250 um per side on a 2-3 mm plate, and say
   whether a typical generator's frequency-tracking range would still lock. Comment on damping and
   heating in a porous coat.

7. Powder consequences. At the W pickup estimated in item 2, would W stay in solution in Cu-30Ni
   powder or appear as W particles, and what would it do to compliance with UNS C71500 (and the
   military specifications that cite it), to seawater corrosion, and to laser powder-bed fusion?

Finish with (a) a direct verdict on W versus Mo for this run, (b) a table of failure mode -> Mo coat
-> W coat (numbers where possible) -> mitigation, and (c) the plate you would choose for this run and
why (solid Mo or TZM, solid W or W-La2O3, W-coated Mo, or a ceramic such as BN, alumina, zirconia or
SiC-coated C/C), naming any ultrasonic-atomization or ultrasonic-melt-processing precedent for it.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
In recent years, W-Cu composite systems have become very interesting subjects due to good electrical and thermal conductivity, high-temperature strength, certain plasticity, and excellent radiation resistance. W-Cu composites are a very important class of materials in applications like PFM (plasma facing materials), functional graded materials (FGM), electronic packaging materials, high-voltage electrical contacts, sweating materials, shaped charge liners, electromagnetic gun-rail materials, kinetic energy penetrators, and radiation shielding/protection. There is no possibility of forming a crystalline structure between these two materials. However, due to the unique properties these materials possess, they can be used by preparing them as a composite. Generally, W-Cu composites are prepared via the conventional powder metallurgy routes, i.e., sintering, hot pressing, hot isostatic pressing, isostatic cold pressing, sintering and infiltration, and microwave sintering. However, these processes have certain limitations, like the inability to produce bulk material, they are expensive, and their adoptability is limited. Here, in this review, we will discuss in detail the fabrication routes of additive manufacturing, and its current progress, challenges, trends, and associated properties obtained. We will also explain the challenges for the additive manufacturing of the composite. We will also compare W-Cu composites to other materials that can challenge them in terms of specific applications or service conditions. The solidification mechanism will be explained for W-Cu composites in additive manufacturing. Finally, we will conclude the progress of additive manufacturing of W-Cu composites to date and suggest future recommendations based on the current challenges in additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
A heat-resistant superalloy from destroyed special equipment was used for further processing to extract valuable metals such as rhenium, nickel, cobalt, tungsten, molybdenum, niobium, tantalum, and others. The need to develop an effective method for the electrochemical dissolution of this superalloy is due to the shortage and high cost of the component metals, especially rhenium. The electrochemical dissolution method is effective for the rapid and complete dissolution of such hard alloys, optimizing the extraction process of valuable components.
In the course of the work, the composition of the unknown superalloy was determined, and the possible grade of the alloy was identified as JS32-VI. For the first time, a comparison of the anodic behavior of the heat-resistant superalloy containing rhenium in various electrolyte solutions, including methanesulfonic acid, was carried out. This comparison helped determine which electrolyte is best suited for dissolving the superalloy and extracting valuable metals from it.
The results showed that solutions containing chloride ions (NaCl and HCl) are the most effective for the electrochemical dissolution of the superalloy. These results are explained by the fact that chloride ions help remove the passive oxide film from the metal surface. Thus, chloride solutions provide more effective dissolution of the superalloy compared to methanesulfonic acid and sulfuric acid.
The key finding of the study is the identification of chloride solutions as the most effective for dissolving the superalloy, which optimizes the process of extracting valuable metals. The application of these methods will contribute to resource conservation and the reduction of production costs, which is important for industries using such materials

Abstract:
An assessment of the tritium (T) inventory in plasma facing components (PFC) during JET T and deuterium-tritium (DT) operations is presented based on the most comprehensive ex situ fuel retention data set on JET PFCs from the 2015-2016 ILW3 operating period is presented. The global fuel retention is 4.19 × 1023 D atoms, 0.19% of injected fuel. The inner divertor remains the region of highest fuel retention (46.5%). The T inventory in PFCs at the end of JET operations is calculated as 7.48 × 1022 atoms and is informative for accountancy, clean-up efficacy and waste liability assessments. The T accumulation rate at the upper inner divertor during JET DT operations has been used to assess the requirements and frequency of operation of a new laser induced desorption diagnostic to be installed on JET for the final DT experiments in 2023.

Abstract:
<jats:p>The transition to lead-free soldering technology has driven significant research into advanced finishing layers with improved thermal stability and controlled interfacial reactivity. ENIG PCB finish is widely used in electronics, particularly in surface-mount technology for printed circuit boards. In the present work, previous studies on the reactivity of electroless Ni-P-Re finishing layers with varying phosphorus content were continued, this time using commercially available SAC305 solder (Sn-3.0Ag-0.5Cu). The addition of rhenium is expected to suppress or eliminate the massive detachment of intermetallic phases from the interface and their migration into the solder. To this end, three surface finish variants with different phosphorus content but constant rhenium content were deposited. The wettability of both Ni-P and Ni-P-Re finishing layers with SAC305 alloy was investigated using the sessile drop method. The obtained systems were subsequently subjected to cyclic heating and cooling to simulate typical operating conditions of electronic devices. The finishing layers, as well as the surface finish/solder systems before and after thermal cycling, were characterized using scanning and transmission electron microscopy together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy to evaluate microstructural and compositional changes. The results revealed a significant influence of both phosphorus content and rhenium addition on the sequence of interfacial phase formation and on the fraction of (Cu,Ni)6Sn5 phase spalling into the solder volume. The presence of both elements strongly affected the formation and thickness of the undesirable Ni2SnP phase at the interface, both immediately after the wetting test and after thermal cycling.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>This study investigates experimentally produced brazed joints between carbon-carbon composite material (CCCM) and tungsten in a vacuum.
The task addressed is to obtain high-temperature brazed joints capable of operating at temperatures of 1400–1600°C in a vacuum under conditions of high thermal cycling loads. Existing methods for joining CCCM with tungsten testify for a virtual lack of experience in brazing such materials, especially for structures of thermal emission equipment.
In this work, a method was used to produce a metallized layer zone with partial melting using a mixture of Ti-Nb-Zr powders on the inner surface of an CCCM sample. Subsequently, the CCCM and tungsten samples were brazed with a Ti-Nb filler metal at a temperature of 1840°C in a vacuum.
The results of microstructural analysis revealed that the brazed joint exhibits a zonal structure. Zone I – a reaction carbide layer (width 10–12 μm), zone II – diffusion layer (width up to 70 μm), zone III – reaction layer adjacent to tungsten (width up to 30 μm). The results of phase formation modeling conducted at a temperature of 1840°C indicate the predominant formation of TiC, NbC, Nb6C5, and Nb2C. Additionally, the distribution of C, Ti, Nb, and W in the brazed joint was determined. The results of the microhardness study confirmed the accuracy of the simulation and showed that microhardness values decrease from Zone I (2300 HV) to Zone III (500–600 HV).
The proposed solutions demonstrate that the metallized layer helps retain solder in the joint gap; reduces thermomechanical stresses; and promotes the formation of a gradual hardness gradient. Together, these characteristics improve the ductile properties of the brazed joint.
The results of this study could be applied in the field of instrument engineering, specifically in the manufacture of cathode components whose emitters are made from ultrafine powders of rare-earth borides or their alloys</jats:p>

Abstract:
A new powder production method has been developed to speed up the search for novel alloys for additive manufacturing. The technique involves an ultrasonically agitated cold crucible installed at the top of a 20 kHz ultrasonic sonotrode. The material is melted with an electric arc and undergoes pulverization with standing wave vibrations. Several different alloys in various forms, including noble and metallic glass alloys, were chosen to test the process. The atomized particles showed exceptional sphericity, while powder output suitable for additive manufacturing reached up to 60%. The AMZ4 metallic glass powder remained amorphous below the 50 μm fraction, while tungsten addition led to crystallization in each fraction. Minor contamination and high Mn and Zn evaporation, especially in the finest particles, was observed in atomized powders. The innovative ultrasonic atomization method appears as a promising tool for material scientists to develop powders with tailored chemical composition, size and structure.

Abstract:
Abstract. This research presents a comprehensive study on the production of aluminum-matrix composite (AMC) powders using ultrasonic atomization for additive manufacturing (AM). The impact of different heat sources—plasma, arc, and induction melting—was evaluated on the processability and resultant properties of the AMC powders, including morphology, size, and composite structure. Additionally, induction melting was considered in terms of process parameters such as pressure difference, nozzle size, and frequency. The analysis of AMC powder processability revealed that the efficiency of the ultrasonic process depended on the selected heat source. The highest efficiency, nearly 50%, was attained with the induction system. All produced AMC powders exhibited high sphericity, with average sizes ranging from 88.2 to 120 µm. However, the desired composite structure was not achieved under tested conditions due to the decrease in SiC particle content from 20% in the feed material to approximately 3.5% in the final AMC powder. Based on these results, the research highlights the potential and limitations of ultrasonic atomization in AMC powder production, emphasizing the need for further optimization to improve powder quality and process efficiency for broader industrial application in AM.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Cemented carbides are essential in applications requiring exceptional hardness and wear resistance. However, the reliance on cobalt as a binder raises concerns related to cost, supply security, and health. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising cobalt-free binders offering favorable mechanical properties and potential grain-growth control. This work presents a new approach for the development of Co-free WC-based cemented carbide employing an HEA binder designed through CALPHAD-guided simulations. An optimized composition corresponding to Al5Cr5Cu10Fe35Mn10Ni35 (at%) alloy is predicted to be FCC-dominant with minimal σ-phase formation and good compatibility with WC. A preliminary batch of powder of the proposed binder was produced by blending elemental powders, arc remelting, and ultrasonic atomization, yielding predominantly spherical particles with a dendritic microstructure. WC–HEA composites (WC–12 wt% HEA) were then prepared by ball milling, pressing, vacuum sintering, and sinter-HIP for a first evaluation of the microstructure and achievable hardness. The microstructure exhibited residual porosity without significant WC grain coarsening. XRD analyses showed the dominant presence of WC, along with FCC and M3W3C phases (M mainly Fe and Mn), indicating thermal interaction between the binder and WC. Despite these effects, the composite achieved a hardness of 1913 HV and retained a fine WC grain size (0.86 μm). The proposed design approach allowed the definition of a promising Co-free binder composition based on HEA with the expected microstructure, which will need further evaluation, especially aimed at investigating toughness properties as a function of the WC content.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>The object of research is the system of electrode blanks used for electrical discharge machining (EDM) of P35 hard alloy components, in particular a pseudo-alloy electrode based on W-Cu, modified with Ni or Co and reinforced with TiC.
The development of modified W-Cu electrodes made it possible to minimize the tool wear rate (TWR) and improve the surface quality of P35 hard alloy components during EDM. To increase the efficiency of W-Cu-based electrodes, the powders were cold pressed at 0.2 MPa at room temperature and sintered-infiltrated at 1200°C in a reducing hydrogen (H2) atmosphere. Copper and nickel acted as metallic catalytic sealants in combination with a dispersed ceramic phase of titanium carbide (TiC). The results show that the modified cobalt-titanium carbide (Co-TiC) composite achieved the highest Vickers microhardness of 326 HV while exhibiting optimal erosion protection. Machining of P35 carbide using a W-Cu-Co-TiC electrode composite resulted in 50% less volumetric wear than using an equivalent nickel electrode composite W-Cu-Ni-TiC. The strong chemical affinity between the cobalt carbide matrix, tungsten, and titanium carbide promotes the development of an elastic microstructural network. The dispersed TiC inclusions attenuate the propagation of thermal shocks, effectively suppressing localized microstructural delamination and grain separation during high-temperature plasma spark interactions.
Synergistic activation of Co and strengthening of TiC directly improve the tribological wear resistance and operational reliability of W-Cu electrodes in contact with refractory carbide substrates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Growing interest in molten salts as effective high-temperature heat-transfer fluids for sustainable energy systems drives a critical need to fundamentally understand the interactions between metals and molten salts. This work utilizes the multimodal microscopy methods of synchrotron X-ray nano-tomography and electron microscopy to investigate the 3D morphological and chemical evolution of two model systems, pure nickel metal and Ni-20Cr binary alloy, in a representative molten salt (KCl-MgCl2 50-50 mol. %, 800 °C). In both systems, unexpected shell-like structures formed due to the presence of more noble tungsten, suggesting a potential route of using Ni-W alloys for enhanced molten-salt corrosion resistance. The binary alloy Ni-20Cr developed a bicontinuous porous structure, reassembling functional porous metals manufactured by dealloying. This work elucidates better mechanistic understanding of corrosion in molten salts, which can contribute to the design of more reliable alloys for molten salt applications including next-generation nuclear and solar power plants and opens the possibility of using molten salts to fabricate functional porous materials.

                    C carbides (WSC) and carburized variants (cWSC) featuring a stabilizing WC surface layer under an energy-reduced, controlled short-circuit GMAW hardfacing process. Thermal exposure is considered as two consecutive stages involving dissolution in the molten droplet and diffusion-dominated dissolution during weld-pool residence. Transient electrical process data and weld-pool surface temperature measurements are used to determine the specific droplet enthalpy and the relevant temperature–time regimes. An analytical model based on the shrinking-core concept is developed to quantify carbide dissolution as a function of particle size and cooling time and is validated experimentally by statistical particle-size analysis and particle-counting methods. The results reveal a pronounced size dependence of dissolution, with particles smaller than approximately 80 µm undergoing extensive degradation largely independent of heat input. Carburized carbides exhibit significantly reduced dissolution compared to conventional eutectoid carbides, retaining an intact WC surface layer throughout processing. Furthermore, dissolution is markedly enhanced in iron-based melts compared to iron-nickel systems, indicating that Fe-Ni matrices in combination with carburized carbides are preferable for minimizing carbide degradation in GMAW hardfacing applications.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Accurate measurement of oxide concentration in molten chloride salts is essential for mitigating impurity-driven corrosion and experimental drift in molten salt experiments and applications. Most reported electrochemical methods have been developed for quiescent baths with stationary working electrodes (WEs) and Ag/AgCl reference electrodes (REs). Here, we evaluate an in-situ oxide sensor with both stationary and rotating WEs to assess the sensitivity and responsiveness of electrochemical sensors to changes in oxide concentrations and flow conditions. Experiments were performed in the eutectic NaCl–KCl system using a Ni/NiO RE and four WEs: nickel, gold, platinum, and tungsten. We compare sensor performance with stationary and rotating WEs and quantify the signal responsiveness and sensitivity of different WEs to oxides. Tungsten and gold exhibited the lowest detection limits, reaching approximately 51 ppm and 143 ppm O
                    <jats:sup>2 −</jats:sup>
                    (w/w), respectively, while platinum and nickel required higher oxide concentrations to produce stable responses. The WE material substantially impacts sensitivity, with W providing the strongest response. Overall, this work furthers the development and improvement of monitoring of oxide concentration in quiescent and flowing molten salt systems relevant to molten-salt reactors and related high-temperature electrochemical processes.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
The 2014–2016 JET results are reviewed in the light of their significance for optimising the ITER research plan for the active and non-active operation. More than 60 h of plasma operation with ITER first wall materials successfully took place since its installation in 2011. New multi-machine scaling of the type I-ELM divertor energy flux density to ITER is supported by first principle modelling. ITER relevant disruption experiments and first principle modelling are reported with a set of three disruption mitigation valves mimicking the ITER setup. Insights of the L–H power threshold in Deuterium and Hydrogen are given, stressing the importance of the magnetic configurations and the recent measurements of fine-scale structures in the edge radial electric. Dimensionless scans of the core and pedestal confinement provide new information to elucidate the importance of the first wall material on the fusion performance. H-mode plasmas at ITER triangularity (H  =  1 at βN ~ 1.8 and n/nGW ~ 0.6) have been sustained at 2 MA during 5 s. The ITER neutronics codes have been validated on high performance experiments. Prospects for the coming D–T campaign and 14 MeV neutron calibration strategy are reviewed.

## pqac-00000006

From text 'matthews2009developmentofdivertor pages 3-4'.

G. Matthews, P. Coad, H. Greuner, M. Hill, T. Hirai, J. Likonen, H. Maier, M. Mayer, R. Neu, V. Philipps, R. Pitts, V. Riccardo, and J. Contributors. Development of divertor tungsten coatings for the jet iter-like wall. Journal of Nuclear Materials, pages 934-937, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.01.239, doi:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.01.239. This article has 71 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes several tungsten coating configurations relevant to carbon-fibre composite (CFC) and graphite components, but it does not provide details about a molybdenum interlayer or CMSII processing. The JET divertor reference configuration is a 14 micrometre W/Re multilayer PVD coating; the figure compares 3 micrometre tungsten on 2D CFC in JET with 0.56 micrometre coatings on fine-grained graphite in ASDEX Upgrade. The W/Re PVD layer was retained as the backup option and was considered useful as a carbon-diffusion barrier that suppresses carbide formation. JUDITH1 testing found no observable damage after 1000 cycles at 0.33 GW m^-2 for 1 ms pulses, while 0.4 GW m^-2 produced slight cracking and melting along in-plane fibres; coating over fibres entering the surface remained undamaged. Thick VPS tungsten coatings of 200–500 micrometres were used on fine-grained graphite, but failures occurred through interface delamination and sub-layer delamination. The authors warn that thick VPS layers can undergo progressive peeling and form droplets that do not wet carbon, potentially increasing tungsten release and affecting machine operation. The excerpt also notes that a 14 micrometre W/Re multilayer had an estimated conservative lifetime of about 60,000 seconds before CFC exposure.

## pqac-00000007

From text 'hirai2009failuremodesof pages 2-4'.

T. Hirai, N. Bekris, J.P. Coad, C. Grisolia, J. Linke, H. Maier, G.F. Matthews, V. Philipps, and E. Wessel. Failure modes of vacuum plasma spray tungsten coating created on carbon fibre composites under thermal loads. Journal of Nuclear Materials, 392:40-44, Jul 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060, doi:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt describes vacuum plasma-sprayed tungsten (VPS-W) on a large carbon-fibre-composite (CFC) block representative of approximately half a JET divertor tile (100 × 300 mm²). The tungsten coating was about 200 µm thick. The CFC consisted of cross-ply PAN-fibre laminates with felt layers as a compliant interlayer; the excerpt does not explicitly identify a molybdenum (Mo) interlayer or discuss CMSII. Electron-beam tests applied ELM-like 1 ms pulses and longer 2 s loads. Under cyclic short-pulse loading, surface damage included cracking, melting at crack edges, small droplets, and peeling or extraction of coating sublayers. Cross-sections showed delamination/removal of the coating one sublayer at a time, attributed to poor mechanical and thermal contact between sublayers. The coating contained seven sublayers, corresponding to individual plasma-torch passes. A pre-existing tensile crack propagated through the full coating thickness, across loaded and unloaded surfaces, perpendicular to the underlying cross-ply fibre bundles; its width was approximately 20 µm. Damage and rising surface temperature were associated with degraded thermal contact and less efficient heat removal. Large-area coatings were more vulnerable than small samples, likely because production created sublayers through less-controlled deposition conditions.

## pqac-00000008

From text 'matthews2009developmentofdivertor pages 1-2'.

G. Matthews, P. Coad, H. Greuner, M. Hill, T. Hirai, J. Likonen, H. Maier, M. Mayer, R. Neu, V. Philipps, R. Pitts, V. Riccardo, and J. Contributors. Development of divertor tungsten coatings for the jet iter-like wall. Journal of Nuclear Materials, pages 934-937, Jun 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.01.239, doi:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.01.239. This article has 71 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

For the JET ITER-like Wall, tungsten coatings were applied to CFC divertor components because replacing the entire divertor with bulk tungsten was not feasible. The principal thick-coating option was a 200 μm tungsten VPS coating with a W/Re interlayer, produced by Plansee. Under steady heat loads, this coating performed at least as well as 5 and 10 μm PVD coatings; under ELM-like loads, VPS performed better, possibly because the short heat pulse did not reach the CFC/coating interface. Greater thickness also provides more margin against normal erosion. However, scaling VPS to realistic tiles and mass production presented risks, since coating performance depends on CFC properties, machining, fibre orientation, surface preparation, torch angle, and cooling between passes. For main-chamber tiles, the selected thin coating was a 10 μm tungsten layer with a Mo interlayer made by CMSII (combined magnetron sputtering and ion implantation), a process developed for industrial-scale production. A 14 μm PVD W/Re multilayer was developed as a VPS fallback; its Re/W layers improve interface ductility with CFC and limit brittle tungsten-carbide formation. The excerpt reports that this multilayer performed well on representative Tile 0 geometry, with no defects after 100 thermal cycles at 4 MW m⁻² for 0.5 s. It does not provide detailed adhesion-strength values or the later VPS delamination/cracking results.

The excerpt concerns the JET ITER-like Wall application of tungsten-coated carbon-fibre composite (CFC) divertor tiles, specifically the outer and inner divertor rows. It identifies a 200 µm vacuum plasma spray tungsten (VPS-W) coating selected for the application. The coating was deposited on two-directional CFC and incorporated a Re/W multilayer interlayer rather than a Mo interlayer. The six-layer interlayer, listed from CFC toward VPS-W, consisted of 10 µm Re, 2 µm W, 3 µm Re, 2 µm W, 2.5 µm Re, and 1 µm W. Its purposes were to act as a carbon diffusion barrier, suppress tungsten-carbide formation, and provide a compliant transition between hard tungsten and CFC. The article attributes potential cracking to residual stresses caused by anisotropic thermal-expansion mismatch; tensile cracks could arise even after manufacture. Under cyclic ELM-like loading, the VPS-W coating failed sub-layer by sub-layer at 0.33 GW/m² for 1 ms pulses. Under longer, steady-state-like pulses, failure occurred above 2700 °C when the Re-containing interlayer melted at the VPS-W/CFC interface. The supplied excerpt does not mention CMSII, measured adhesion strength, delamination terminology, or a Mo interlayer.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'hirai2009failuremodesof pages 4-5'.

T. Hirai, N. Bekris, J.P. Coad, C. Grisolia, J. Linke, H. Maier, G.F. Matthews, V. Philipps, and E. Wessel. Failure modes of vacuum plasma spray tungsten coating created on carbon fibre composites under thermal loads. Journal of Nuclear Materials, 392:40-44, Jul 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060, doi:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns a 200-µm-thick vacuum plasma-sprayed tungsten (VPS-W) coating on a two-dimensional carbon-fibre composite (CFC), using a W/Re multilayer interlayer—not a Mo interlayer. It evaluates ELM-like short transient pulses and longer steady-state thermal loads. During short pulses, damage consisted mainly of small surface droplets and peeling of VPS-W sublayers; the power-density damage threshold was below 0.33 GW/m² for 1 ms. Horizontal cracks formed beneath the coating in the CFC because of poor mechanical stability, extending several millimetres around tensile cracks. These cracks reduced thermal contact, increasing surface temperature and lowering the cooling rate. Under steady-state loading, local overheating above parallel fibre bundles caused interlayer melting. Mutual diffusion and formation of W–Re alloy and/or tungsten carbide reduced the effective melting temperature, with reported melting points down to approximately 2825°C and 2715°C. Molten tungsten alloy poorly wetted the carbon, producing craters, cavities, open carbon surfaces, and separation. The excerpt does not provide CMSII-specific results, quantitative adhesion strength, a Mo-interlayer design, or a dedicated delamination measurement; it does, however, document sublayer peeling, cracking in the CFC, interfacial failure, and thermally induced coating destruction.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'hirai2009failuremodesof pages 5-5'.

T. Hirai, N. Bekris, J.P. Coad, C. Grisolia, J. Linke, H. Maier, G.F. Matthews, V. Philipps, and E. Wessel. Failure modes of vacuum plasma spray tungsten coating created on carbon fibre composites under thermal loads. Journal of Nuclear Materials, 392:40-44, Jul 2009. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060, doi:10.1016/j.jnucmat.2009.03.060. This article has 43 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

The excerpt concerns failure modes of vacuum plasma-sprayed tungsten (VPS-W) coatings applied to carbon-fibre composites (CFCs) under thermal loads, in the context of the JET ITER-like Wall (ILW) programme. It reports that experimental heat-load observations identified serious failure risks in thick tungsten coatings. At locally overheated surfaces parallel to the fibre bundles, formation of W–Re alloy and/or tungsten carbide reduced the coating melting temperature. The reported damage thresholds were approximately 2825 °C for W–Re alloy and 2715 °C for tungsten carbide. Based on repeated experimental observations of failure in thick W coatings under heat loads, the ILW Project excluded the 200 μm VPS-W coating from its baseline. The excerpt states that thinner PVD-W coatings were instead being developed and qualified for the ILW. This passage does not provide specific details on a molybdenum interlayer, CMSII testing, quantitative adhesion strength, delamination morphology, or crack dimensions. It therefore supports conclusions about VPS-W coating thickness, thermally induced degradation, alloy/carbide formation, and the resulting change from 200 μm VPS-W toward thinner PVD-W coatings, but not a complete account of the requested coating architecture or all mechanical failure mechanisms.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Superhydrophobic and superoleophilic hierarchical urchin-like copper oxide powders were synthesized by a facile one-step method without the use of low-surface-energy modifiers. The selective wettability of the powders toward water and oil makes them suitable for oil adsorption from oil-in-water emulsions. In addition, the hierarchical CuO structures were grown in situ on a stainless-steel mesh, which was used for the separation of heavy oil–water mixtures. The synergistic combination of micro-/nanoscale roughness and a reduction in the polar component of surface free energy through hydroxylation of the copper oxide surface likely leads to a significant decrease in wettability and the development of superhydrophobic and superoleophilic properties, as evidenced by a static water contact angle of 161.1° ± 2° and an oil contact angle of 0°, measured on the CuO-coated mesh surface. The superhydrophobic copper oxide particles demonstrated a high oil adsorption selectivity greater than 19. The immiscible chloroform/water mixture was separated via a simple filtration method using a superhydrophobic/superoleophilic copper oxide–coated mesh filter, achieving a separation efficiency of approximately 98% and a chloroform permeation flux of about 7300 L m⁻² h⁻¹. In addition, copper oxide powder showed promising potential as a selective oil adsorbent for the treatment of oil-in-water emulsions and the cleanup of oil spills when used in the form of sorbent booms or pillows.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The remelting method is introduced to improve the properties of the as-sprayed NiCrBSi coatings. In this work, tungsten carbide (WC) was selected as reinforcement and the as-sprayed and remelted NiCrBSi/WC composite coatings were investigated by X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, hardness test and tribology test. After spraying, WC particles are evenly distributed in the coating. The remelting process induced the decarburizing reaction of WC, resulting in the formation of dispersed W2C. The dispersed W2C particles play an important role in the dispersion strengthening. Meanwhile, the pores and lamellar structures are eliminated in the remelted NiCrBSi/WC composite coating. Due to these two advantages, the hardness and the high-temperature wear resistance of the remelted NiCrBSi/WC composite coating are significantly improved compared with those with an as-sprayed NiCrBSi coating; the as-sprayed NiCrBSi coating, as-sprayed NiCrBSi/WC composite coating and remelted NiCrBSi/WC composite coating have average hardness of 673.82, 785.14, 1061.23 HV, and their friction coefficients are 0.3418, 0.3261, 0.2431, respectively. The wear volume of the remelted NiCrBSi/WC composite coating is only one-third of that of the as-sprayed NiCrBSi coating.

Remelted alloy rods were positioned above the sonotrode, and the rod ends were melted by an arc torch onto the sonotrode surface. Ultrasonic vibration promoted outward ejection of smaller molten droplets, which cooled and solidified during flight before being collected as powder. The excerpt does not identify the sonotrode material, report molybdenum contamination, specify a sonotrode plate material, or discuss dissolution or erosion of the plate/sonotrode during atomization. The remelted alloy itself showed copper-enriched bright dendritic regions and manganese segregation at dendrite boundaries. The atomized powder was generally spherical, with very small amounts of irregular features and submicron satellites. Thus, this passage provides process details relevant to AMAZEMET rePOWDER-style ultrasonic atomization but offers no evidence for assessing sonotrode composition, molybdenum transfer, plate dissolution, or erosion.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Plastic deformation in body-centred cubic (bcc) metals and alloys is conventionally mediated by screw dislocations. Their temperature-sensitive motion is attributed to a steep rise in strength with decreasing temperature that constricts plastic zones at crack tips, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition
                    <jats:sup>1</jats:sup>
                    . Here we evaluated the mechanical properties of group IV–V bcc refractory alloys with similar electronic structures at 20 K and found that these materials instead exhibit a plateau in tensile yield strength and fracture toughness as a function of temperature, with no apparent ductile-to-brittle transition. This behaviour arises from the global activation of twinning and an ω-phase transformation, which nucleate dislocations at interfaces before global dislocation motion. The initial mechanism is temperature insensitive and controls yielding, thereby preventing a crack-tip plastic zone from constricting with decreasing temperature.
                  </jats:p>

URL: https://doi.org/10.2320/matertrans.44.358, doi:10.2320/matertrans.44.358. This article has 20 citations and is from a peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt does not report a numerical dissolution rate, recession rate, or diffusion coefficient for tungsten or molybdenum dissolving into liquid nickel or Ni-based melts. Instead, it provides compositional and thermodynamic observations concerning dissolution and redistribution during isothermal holding at 1773 K. For the investigated W–Mo–Ni–Fe alloys, molybdenum was inferred to dissolve into the matrix phase more readily than tungsten: the apparent activity coefficient of Mo in the matrix exceeded that of W by a factor of 2.7, and Mo was stated to dissolve more easily than W. The combined W+Mo concentration in the matrix was approximately 13.1–13.9 at% for the two alloys. During longer holding times, Mo concentration in the liquid increased while W concentration decreased, indicating preferential partitioning and dissolution behavior. The authors associated increasing Mo content in the liquid with W–Mo grain growth and subsequent intermetallic-phase precipitation during cooling. The excerpt also compares Ni–Mo and Ni–W thermodynamics, noting that MoNi formation during cooling would be faster than formation of W–Ni intermetallics because of the relative eutectic and transformation temperatures. These are qualitative/measured composition and phase-transformation findings, not kinetic dissolution measurements; no liquid-metal penetration distance, mass-loss rate, interface recession rate, or W/Mo diffusion coefficient is given here.

This excerpt does not report measured dissolution rates, recession rates, or diffusion coefficients for tungsten or molybdenum dissolving into liquid nickel or Ni-based melts. It instead provides equilibrium phase-diagram and compositional information relevant to dissolution limits. For the binary W–Ni system, the eutectic temperature is 1768 K; the W eutectic composition is 20.7 at%, while the W solubility limit in the Ni solid solution at that temperature is 17.5 at%, giving a composition difference of 3.2 at%. For Mo–Ni, the eutectic temperature is 1590 K; the Mo eutectic composition is 35.0 at%, and the Mo solubility limit in the Ni solid solution at the eutectic temperature is 28.4 at%, giving a larger difference of 6.6 at%. The authors interpret this larger Mo composition difference as greater Mo supersaturation during phase transformation and therefore a higher potential for Mo–Ni intermetallic formation than for W–Ni. In W–Mo–Ni–Fe alloys, Mo was reported to be more soluble in the matrix than W by approximately a factor of 2.6 after short holding at 1773 K. These data are thermodynamic/compositional rather than kinetic measurements and cannot be converted into dissolution rates or diffusion coefficients without additional time-dependent experiments.

It discusses tungsten carbide (WC) particles in oxygen-bearing nickel melts and describes the dissolution mechanism qualitatively. A coherent, persistent WC reaction layer forms around immersed particles, consistent with a shrinking-core mechanism. This rim creates a solid-state diffusion path with very low diffusivity, substantially reducing the effective diffusivity compared with transport through the liquid. High oxygen activity in nickel melts also lowers carbon solubility and increases the viscosity of the liquid boundary layer, thereby impeding carbon transfer from WC into the melt. The excerpt emphasizes that this stable interfacial layer constricts liquid continuity and strongly retards intergranular infiltration and particle-edge removal. Consequently, the passage supports a conclusion of diffusion- and reaction-layer-controlled, relatively slow WC dissolution in oxygen-bearing Ni melts, but it provides no numerical value that can be converted into a W dissolution rate or recession rate. It contains no data on molybdenum dissolution, Mo diffusion coefficients, or quantitative W transport in Ni-based liquids.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Controlling hydrogen isotope retention is a critical challenge for plasma-facing materials (PFMs) in fusion reactors. Chemical vapor deposited tungsten (CVD-W), featuring columnar grain structures, has attracted increasing attention as a candidate PFM. However, its surface blistering and deuterium (D) retention behavior under fusion-relevant, complex irradiation conditions remain insufficiently understood. In this work, CVD-W and ITER-like forged W both with grains elongated normal to the exposed surface were irradiated with pure D and mixed D + 5% He plasma, with and without prior W self-ion irradiation at damage levels of 0.2 and 2 dpa. Compared with ITER-like W, CVD-W exhibits substantially enhanced tolerance to D-induced surface blister formation and markedly reduced D retention under pure D plasma exposure. Regardless of displacement damage, He seeding, or their combination, CVD-W consistently retains less D than ITER-like W across all irradiation sequences studied. This persistently low D retention in CVD-W is primarily associated with its lower defect density (e.g. fewer grain boundaries) and a blister-resistant <001> surface texture that limits blister-related D trapping. Furthermore, displacement damage and He seeding effectively suppress surface blistering, but exert opposing individual effects on D retention in both materials. Their combined effect shows a clear dependence on D fluence and material microstructure. This work highlights the advantages of CVD-W in suppressing hydrogen isotope retention under complex irradiation environments and provides valuable insights for the selection and microstructural design of advanced PFMs with improved resistance to hydrogen-induced blistering and reduced retention.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Silicon electrochemistry has the potential to advance sustainable energy solutions by offering environmentally friendly and secure technologies that can contribute to the low-carbon economy. Electrochemical methods use electrons directly as reducing agents, eliminating the need for harmful chemicals and offering simpler, one-step, process control. Silicon itself is the second most abundant element in the earth's crust, is nontoxic, and is a robust material offering high efficiencies in solar photovoltaics. As such, silicon currently dominates the solar energy market and could continue to do so for the next few decades. This review summarizes recent achievements in the molten salt electrochemistry of silicon, highlighting subjects of technological significance such as the production of silicon by silica electro-deoxidation, the formation of photoactive layers, silicon electrorefining, and the synthesis of semiconductors as well as nanostructures for energy storage applications. The review highlights future opportunities and challenges such as the production of highly pure silicon, the creation of carbon-free anodes for oxygen production, and silicon electrodeposition from gaseous precursors.

From text '宁先进2026processoptimizationfor pages 7-9'.

谢铮， 汪龙龙， 谭成文， 于晓东， 宁先进. Process optimization for preparing uniform and dense tungsten coatings on throat liners by cvd. Unknown journal, 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20250595, doi:10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20250595.

The excerpt reports properties of a CVD tungsten coating deposited on a C/C composite throat liner. The coating is described as dense, essentially free of internal defects, and capable of penetrating substrate pores to form a mechanical anchoring bond. Its measured density is 19.17 g/cm3, close to the theoretical density of tungsten (19.35 g/cm3). Tensile testing gives an approximate coating–substrate tensile strength of 4.6 MPa. The fracture occurs mainly within the porous C/C substrate rather than at the tungsten/C/C interface, and carbon particles and fibers adhere to the fracture surface, indicating excellent bonding. The excerpt does not state the coating thickness, does not identify WF6 as the precursor, and does not report W2C or other carbide formation at the interface. Metallography instead describes a polycrystalline coating with an initial competitive-growth zone adjacent to the substrate and an upper columnar-grain zone. The interface morphology is illustrated in the cited figure, but no additional carbide-phase analysis is provided in the text.

## pqac-00000022

From text '宁先进2026processoptimizationfor pages 1-2'.

谢铮， 汪龙龙， 谭成文， 于晓东， 宁先进. Process optimization for preparing uniform and dense tungsten coatings on throat liners by cvd. Unknown journal, 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20250595, doi:10.12442/j.issn.1002-185x.20250595.

The excerpt concerns atmospheric-pressure CVD (APCVD) of tungsten coatings for rocket-engine throat liners, using high-purity WF6 and H2 as precursor gases. It states that CVD is suitable for complex-shaped substrates because it can produce high-purity, dense tungsten coatings with minimal surface defects, good uniformity, and strong substrate adhesion. Compared with low-pressure CVD, APCVD provides a higher tungsten deposition rate. The study optimizes reactor geometry using CFD and experiments; the configuration combining an integrated gas-distribution device with a flow-guide baffle improves radial gas diffusion, removes vortices in the liner region, and increases deposition-rate uniformity while slightly improving WF6 utilization. However, the supplied pages do not identify the substrate specifically as a C/C carbon-carbon composite, nor do they report coating thickness, measured density, bonding strength, quantitative adhesion strength, or evidence of W2C carbide formation at the coating/interface. The excerpt only indicates that coating compactness, thickness uniformity, deposition efficiency, and adhesion are important performance considerations. It also notes that tungsten deposition occurs through the H2/WF6 reduction system and is primarily associated with disproportionation reactions involving tungsten subfluorides such as WF4, but no interfacial carbide phase is discussed.
